_label: Evidence archive: the approach to the Ansel Adams organisation (8-9 August 2008)

identified_by.content: Evidence archive: the approach to the Ansel Adams organisation (8-9 August 2008)

content: The earliest documents held in this collection: two messages sent within about twenty minutes of each other on the evening of 2008-08-08 to the Ansel Adams organisation, one carrying eight loose photographs of the print and one carrying the archive later sent to the auction house. They precede the museum letter by two days and the auction house by five, and they identify the body that letter miscalls the Ansel Adams Museum in San Francisco. The message carrying the archive retains its original Hotmail headers; the other has been rewritten by a later platform, and their relative order is not settled.

referred_to_by.content: Two outbound messages to the same named representative at anseladams.com, sent within about twenty minutes of each other on the evening of 2008-08-08 Pacific time, from the studio principal's then-current hotmail.com mailbox. The first as the headers order them, under the subject 'Ansel Adams San Francisco', carries eight loose JPEG photographs of the Ansel Adams print. The second, under the subject 'Ansel Adams Visits SanFrancisco', carries a single attachment: the archive San Francisco.zip, byte-identical to the copy the studio holds and to the one sent to the auction house six days later. Both describe the camera as a 1.3 megapixel FujiFilm, both invite a telephone call in preference to email, both give a telephone number, and both close for the love of Art. Together they are the earliest documents held in this collection, preceding the approach to the museum photography department by two days and the approach to the auction house by five.

The two messages are not equally well evidenced, and the difference is the most important thing in this record. The message carrying the archive retains its original Hotmail headers: an X-Originating-IP stamped by the sending provider, a Date bearing a real local offset of minus seven hours, a GUID-style MIME boundary of the kind Windows Live Hotmail generated, and no Message-ID, Thread-Index, Content-Language or Exchange organisation headers at all. The message carrying the loose photographs has the opposite profile: its Date is normalised to UTC, and it carries a Message-ID whose host is Exchange Online, together with Thread-Index and X-MS-Exchange-Organization headers. Exchange Online did not exist in 2008. So one of these two files has passed through a later platform that rewrote its headers, and the other has not. The archive message is, on its headers, a 2008 artefact. The photographs message is a 2008 message as preserved by a present-day mailbox.

A period marker in the archive message, stated for what it is worth. Its footer advertises the Windows Live Hotmail Mobile Summer Games Trivia Contest, linking to gowindowslive.com. The Beijing Olympic Games opened on 2008-08-08, the date the message bears, and ran to 2008-08-24. A promotional footer tied to that event is consistent with the stated date and would be an odd thing to reconstruct afterwards. It is corroboration of period rather than of the particular day, and it is not independent of the sender, since the footer travelled with the message he sent.

Their order is not settled, and this record does not settle it. The headers place the photographs message about twenty minutes before the archive message. The texts point the other way. The archive message reads as a first delivery: it opens with a greeting and an enquiry after the recipient, describes the photographs as the best the writer could manage, and states a telephone number plainly. The photographs message reads as a second attempt: it says the number is being given 'again', and sends eight of the eleven frames loose rather than archived, which is what a sender does when an archive has not worked. Against that, the two messages give telephone numbers differing in a single digit, so one of them contains a typing error and neither can be used to order them. The honest position is that two messages were sent to the same person within twenty-odd minutes on one evening, that the timestamp of one of them has been rewritten by a later system, and that which came first is not established. Nothing in this collection depends on the answer.

The archive ties this approach to the auction-house record, and does so by content rather than by assertion. The attachment to the 2008-08-08 message is byte-identical to San Francisco.zip, whose SHA-256 the auction-house record already published as the 3 MB attachment sent to the Photographs department on 2008-08-14. The same archive therefore went to the Ansel Adams organisation six days before it went to the trade. Its eleven frames carry EXIF DateTimeOriginal values running from 2008-08-08 00:05:33 to 00:10:22, a single session of about five minutes; the EXIF camera model is FUJIFILM FinePix1300, which agrees with both messages' description of a 1.3 megapixel camera. The eight loose photographs in the other message are byte-identical to eight members of that same archive. Three frames, DSCF0014, DSCF0015 and DSCF0023, were not sent loose. DSCF0020, the frame composing the print with Warhol's philosophy, was sent both ways.

It answers an open question in the museum record, and the two records corroborate each other. The museum letter of 2008-08-11 reports that its writer is in contact with a named person at what he calls 'the Ansel Adams Musem in SanFrancisco'. The museum record notes that no institution of that name was operating in San Francisco in 2008, the Ansel Adams Center for Photography having closed in 2001, and left open which body was meant. These messages identify it, and the museum letter, now held as a file, names the person in full, so the identification no longer rests on inference at all. They are addressed to a named representative at anseladams.com and they predate the museum letter, which is the order that letter's own past tense requires. The misnaming is resolved as a misnaming: the organisation approached bore the photographer's name and was not a San Francisco museum. The weight lies in the independence of the artefacts. The museum letter is held as a screenshot of a mail client; these are held as mailbox exports. Neither was produced from the other, neither needed to mention the other, and they agree on a checkable fact.

Contact began before either message. The photographs message gives a telephone number 'again', and the archive message opens 'How are you doing', asks nothing and explains nothing about who is writing or why, and offers the photographs as though they had been asked for. Both presume a relationship already established. So the engagement with the Adams organisation began before 2008-08-08, and on the evidence of both messages it began by telephone. Nothing of that earlier contact is held: no note, no call record, no reply from the organisation to anything. The earliest documents in this collection are therefore not the beginning of the engagement they document, and no claim about a first approach should rest on them.

The subject lines, and what is not yet in them. These two messages are headed 'Ansel Adams San Francisco' and 'Ansel Adams Visits SanFrancisco'. The messages of 2008-08-11 and 2008-08-14, to the museum and to the auction house, are headed 'Ansel Adams Finds Art in SanFrancisco', and the auction house's replies carry that subject forward. So across six days the heading moves from a plain statement of the subject, through a personification of the photographer as a visitor, to a claim that he finds Art there. The progression is recorded and not interpreted. It is consistent with a framing that developed over that week, and equally consistent with a writer trying different headings on different correspondents; nothing held distinguishes the two. The art-inflected heading is not present at the earliest date.

The sign-off, moved back. The valediction for the love of Art closes both messages of 2008-08-08, and so predates by two days the earliest previously documented use of it. The auction-house record treats the phrase at length, as the studio's own adaptation of the title of Damien Hirst's For the Love of God, and observes that it closed both approaches of August 2008 and was therefore a settled signature rather than a one-off. That observation is strengthened: the phrase now closes four messages, to three organisations, across six days, and is present in the earliest documents the collection holds. What it is not, here as there, is a reference anyone was invited to see. The studio's account of the Hirst adaptation is its own, given in 2026, and is reported as that account rather than as a fact these messages establish.

What these documents establish, and what they do not. They establish that by the evening of 2008-08-08 the studio principal held the Ansel Adams print, had photographed it earlier that day, and was sending those photographs to the organisation bearing the photographer's name; that the archive later sent to the auction house existed in its final form by that evening; that the contact followed an earlier approach made by telephone; and that the sign-off used throughout the August 2008 outreach was in use from the earliest documented moment. They do not touch Metaconceptual Art, which is named in neither. They do not describe the print, the photographs or the approach as an artwork, a performance or a project of any kind: one message offers assistance, the other asks after the recipient and sends files. And they carry no designation of the auction, which had been proposed to nobody when they were written.

Redaction and scope. Following this collection's convention, the representative at the Adams organisation, who was addressed in an official capacity, is identified by role only; their given name and mailbox are withheld pending consent and retained in the studio's private copy. Both correspondents' mailbox addresses are replaced, and the studio principal's telephone numbers are withheld as personal data, though the fact that two numbers are given, that they differ in one digit, and that one is given 'again', is preserved because it bears on the order of the messages. The final octet of the sending provider's X-Originating-IP stamp is withheld; the header itself and the rest of its value are retained, because the presence of that stamp is what distinguishes the two files' provenance and is the point of the record. The domain anseladams.com is deliberately retained: the identity of the organisation approached is what gives the record its weight. No endorsement by that organisation of this project, of Metaconceptual Art, or of any claim in this collection is implied or should be inferred. It was asked in September 2026 whether it retained either message. On 2026-09-07 its customer support team, identified here by role only, replied that the organisation changed email servers in 2015 and lost all email from before 2015, and so could not help. That is a negative with a stated scope: the organisation holds no email of 2008 at all, so its inability to confirm these messages says nothing either way about whether they were received. It said nothing else about them. The unredacted originals are not published; their SHA-256 values are, so the held files can later be shown to be unaltered without their contents being disclosed.
